title: Set up your environment: a local multi-node lab
description: Run several Python processes on localhost ports as 'nodes' and start/stop them with one helper.
outcome: You can start N independent nodes on 127.0.0.1, health-check them over HTTP, and stop them cleanly.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux; macOS on Apple silicon and Windows 11 expected), stdlib only, installed with the canonical commands in ../shared/WORKSTATION-SETUP.md. No network beyond localhost. Optional containers (Podman first) and a two-machine run: documentation/OPTIONAL-SETUP.md (pending).
overview: A 'node' here is just a separate OS process with its own port; that is enough to practise real network calls, failures and timeouts on one laptop.
prerequisites: A terminal; curl is handy but optional

glossary.meaning: One independently running process that communicates only by sending messages over the network.
A cheap endpoint (here GET /health) that proves the node is up and answering.
The number that identifies one listening process on a host (8001, 8002, ...).

concepts: Each node = its own process, memory and port; they share nothing but the network.
Start-up is asynchronous: poll a health endpoint instead of sleeping a fixed time.
Bind to 127.0.0.1 for local labs; use 0.0.0.0 only inside containers.

steps.title: Install Python 3.12 and get the files
steps.detail: Full workstation setup: ../shared/WORKSTATION-SETUP.md. Install Python 3.12, copy labs/L100/01-setup-local-lab into a folder, cd into it and create a virtual environment (no packages to install).
steps.mac:
brew install python@3.12
cd 01-setup-local-lab
python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
python --version
steps.windows:
winget install -e --id Python.Python.3.12
cd 01-setup-local-lab
py -3.12 -m venv .venv; .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
$env:PYTHONUTF8 = "1"
python --version

steps.ifNot: Windows: Activate.ps1 blocked → `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned`. macOS: `python3.12` not found → use `$(brew --prefix)/bin/python3.12`.

steps.title: Run one node by hand
steps.detail: Start one node, then fetch http://127.0.0.1:8001/health from a second terminal or a browser; stop it with Ctrl+C.
steps.mac:
python node.py --name node1 --port 8001
# 2nd terminal:
curl http://127.0.0.1:8001/health
steps.windows:
python node.py --name node1 --port 8001
# 2nd terminal (curl.exe, not the PowerShell curl alias):
curl.exe http://127.0.0.1:8001/health
steps.expected: `{"node": "node1", "port": 8001, "pid": ...}`; Ctrl+C stops it on both OSes.
steps.ifNot: 'Address already in use' (macOS) or `[WinError 10048]` (Windows) → pick another port with --port.

steps.title: Start, check and stop 3 nodes
steps.detail: `python lab.py demo 3` starts 3 node processes, polls /health, then terminates and reaps them.
steps.expected: Three 'nodeN up on port 800N -> /health OK' lines, then 'stopped 3 nodes'.
steps.ifNot: A port is busy → macOS: `LAB_BASE_PORT=18001 python lab.py demo 3`; Windows: `$env:LAB_BASE_PORT=18001; python lab.py demo 3`.

steps.title: Leave nodes running
steps.detail: `start` saves the PIDs to .lab_nodes.json; `status` reads them; `stop` (from any terminal) stops them by PID.
steps.mac:
python lab.py start 3
python lab.py status
python lab.py stop
steps.windows:
python lab.py start 3
python lab.py status
python lab.py stop
steps.expected: status prints one health JSON per node; stop prints 'stopped 3 nodes'.
steps.ifNot: If status fails, a node died: check the port is free and rerun start. On Windows, closing the terminal that ran `start` also ends the nodes.

steps.title: Run the tests and the tryIt script
steps.detail: `python -m unittest -v` (4 tests: start/health/stop, stop by saved PID, second bind on the same port fails, health by host), then `python try_it.py`.
steps.expected: Ran 4 tests ... OK; try_it.py prints the two tryIt results below.
steps.ifNot: A firewall or proxy blocking localhost is the usual cause; allow loopback traffic (the labs already bypass proxies).

equivalents: Same idea in Go: one process per node running `http.ListenAndServe(":8001", nil)`.
Same idea in Node.js: `http.createServer(handler).listen(8001)` per process.
Same idea with containers: one Compose service per node (compose.yaml, Podman first; Docker Desktop is an equivalent with its own licence terms).
Process managers (e.g. systemd units, Windows services) do what lab.py does: start, stop and supervise many processes.
inRealSystems: Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes call an HTTP endpoint such as /healthz (200-399 = success); Docker Compose runs one service per node; Go's http.ListenAndServe is the same one-process-one-port pattern.
useWhen: Use it to learn failure handling and run fast, dependency-free tests on one machine; avoid it for real network loss, latency or partitions, for performance measurement, and beyond localhost (http.server is not for production).
simulatorVsReal: All nodes share one machine (no real loss or partitions). The optional two-machine run (documentation/OPTIONAL-SETUP.md) has not run on real hardware.
caution: http.server is not recommended for production (Python docs). Keep nodes bound to 127.0.0.1. The optional container and LAN paths bind 0.0.0.0 — only on a trusted private network: /health has no authentication (documentation/OPTIONAL-SETUP.md).

checkYourself.q: Why does lab.py poll /health instead of calling time.sleep(1)?
checkYourself.a: Start-up time varies; polling waits just long enough and detects nodes that never start.

checkYourself.q: What happens if two nodes are started on port 8001?
checkYourself.a: The second bind fails ('Address already in use'); that node never becomes healthy (tryIt 1).

checkYourself.q: Why must the container version bind 0.0.0.0 but the laptop version 127.0.0.1?
checkYourself.a: Inside a container traffic arrives on the container's network interface, not its loopback; on the laptop, loopback-only keeps the demo private.

title: Two services talking over HTTP
description: Service A calls service B over HTTP (stdlib http.server + urllib) and measures latency.
outcome: You can expose an HTTP endpoint, call it from another service, handle a non-2xx answer, and measure call latency correctly.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only; no network access needed beyond localhost. macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (install: lesson 1)
overview: A remote call looks like a function call but is two messages over a network: a request and a response, either of which can be slow or lost.

glossary.meaning: Client sends one message, waits, server sends one message back.
Time from sending the request to having the full response.
Remote procedure call: code on one node calling a function on another.

concepts: Measure durations with a monotonic clock (time.perf_counter), never wall-clock time.
Non-2xx answers are normal results you must handle (urllib raises HTTPError).
Every remote call needs a timeout — even this first one passes timeout=2.0.

steps.expected: 5 lines 'A -> B ... -> 200 ...', one '-> 404', and a latency summary.
steps.ifNot: ImportError → you are not on Python 3.7+; check `python --version`.

steps.expected: Single-digit ms on localhost; the first call is often slowest.
steps.ifNot: Hundreds of ms usually means a proxy/VPN or antivirus is inspecting loopback.

"""L100: service A calls service B over HTTP (request/response) and measures latency.

python two_services.py   # starts B on a free localhost port, A sends 5 requests + 1 bad one
"""
import json, statistics, time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlsplit

from helpers import OPENER, QuietHandler, serve  # plumbing: quiet handler, reply(), server thread

PRICES = {"apple": 3, "pear": 4, "plum": 5}


class ServiceB(QuietHandler):
    """Service B: GET /price?item=apple -> 200 {"item": "apple", "price": 3}; unknown -> 404."""
    def do_GET(self):  # request message in (method + target) -> one response message out
        item = parse_qs(urlsplit(self.path).query).get("item", [""])[0]
        if item in PRICES:
            self.reply(200, {"item": item, "price": PRICES[item]})  # 2xx = success
        else:
            self.reply(404, {"error": f"unknown item {item!r}"})  # 4xx = client asked wrongly


def start_b(port=0):  # port 0 = let the OS pick a free port
    return serve(ServiceB, port)


def call_b(base_url, item, timeout=2.0):
    """Service A's side (the RPC stub): one request, one response. Returns (json, latency_ms)."""
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # latency: monotonic clock, can't jump back like time.time()
    with OPENER.open(f"{base_url}/price?item={item}", timeout=timeout) as resp:  # always a timeout
        data = json.load(resp)  # marshalling: JSON bytes on the wire -> Python dict
    return data, (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000


def main():
    b = start_b()
    url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{b.server_port}"
    print(f"service B listening on {url}")
    latencies = []
    for item in ["apple", "pear", "plum", "apple", "pear"]:
        data, ms = call_b(url, item)
        latencies.append(ms)
        print(f"A -> B  GET /price?item={item:<5} -> 200 {data}  ({ms:.1f} ms)")
    try:
        call_b(url, "kiwi")
    except HTTPError as e:  # errors are results: urllib raises non-2xx; handle 404 as an outcome
        print(f"A -> B  GET /price?item=kiwi  -> {e.code} {json.load(e)}")
    print(f"latency ms: min={min(latencies):.1f} median={statistics.median(latencies):.1f} "
          f"max={max(latencies):.1f}")  # median, not mean: a few slow calls skew the average
    b.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

title: Timeouts: fail fast instead of hanging
description: Make B slow; see A wait without a timeout and fail fast with one; pick a timeout from latency percentiles.
outcome: You can put a timeout on every remote call, recognise the timeout exception, and choose a value from measured latency.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only; no network access needed beyond localhost. macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (install: lesson 1)
overview: Without a timeout a caller waits as long as the slowest dependency — possibly forever — while holding threads, sockets and memory.

glossary.meaning: Maximum time a client waits for an operation (a duration).
A point in time after which the client stops waiting (timeout = deadline - now).
Latency that 99.9% of requests beat; 0.1% are slower.

concepts: Set a timeout on every remote call: urlopen without one falls back to the global socket default (no timeout unless you set one), and gRPC sets no deadline by default.
Pick the timeout from the dependency's latency: accept a false-timeout rate (e.g. 0.1%) and use that percentile (p99.9).
urlopen's timeout is per blocking socket operation, not a total budget for the call.

code:
"""L100: a slow service B; A without a timeout waits as long as B takes, A with one fails fast.

python timeouts.py
"""
import math, random, statistics, time
from urllib.error import URLError
from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlsplit

from helpers import OPENER, QuietHandler, serve  # plumbing: quiet handler, reply(), server thread


class SlowB(QuietHandler):
    """GET /work?delay=2.0 -> sleeps `delay` seconds, then answers 200 ok."""
    def do_GET(self):
        time.sleep(float(parse_qs(urlsplit(self.path).query).get("delay", ["0"])[0]))
        try:  # a client timeout does NOT stop the server: B finishes the work anyway
            self.reply(200, b"ok")
        except OSError:
            pass  # client already gave up and closed the socket


def start_b():
    return serve(SlowB)


def call(url, timeout=None):
    """timeout=None -> no client timeout (blocks until B answers, possibly forever)."""
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        kwargs = {} if timeout is None else {"timeout": timeout}  # timeout = max wait per socket op
        with OPENER.open(url, **kwargs) as r:
            return f"{r.status} {r.read().decode()}", time.perf_counter() - t0
    except (TimeoutError, URLError) as e:  # fail fast. read: TimeoutError, connect: URLError
        return f"FAILED {type(e).__name__}", time.perf_counter() - t0


def choose_timeout(seed=7, false_timeout_rate=0.001):
    """Pick the value from data: the latency percentile matching an acceptable false-timeout
    rate (0.1% -> p99.9)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)  # stand-in for B's measured latencies: lognormal around 40 ms
    samples = [rng.lognormvariate(math.log(0.040), 0.35) for _ in range(10_000)]
    q = statistics.quantiles(samples, n=1000)  # q[i] = p((i+1)/10), e.g. q[998] = p99.9
    print(f"B latency: p50={q[499]*1000:.0f} ms  p99={q[989]*1000:.0f} ms  p99.9={q[998]*1000:.0f} ms")
    return round(q[round((1 - false_timeout_rate) * 1000) - 1], 3)


def main():
    b = start_b()
    url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{b.server_port}/work?delay=2.0"
    print("B takes 2.0 s to answer.")
    for timeout in (None, 0.5):
        result, took = call(url, timeout)
        print(f"A timeout={str(timeout):<4} -> {result:<20} after {took:.1f} s")
    print(f"suggested timeout for A->B: {choose_timeout()} s")
    b.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

troubleshooting.symptom: Timeout shows up as URLError instead of TimeoutError
troubleshooting.action: Timeouts while connecting are wrapped in URLError; while reading they raise TimeoutError. Catch both.
The timeout is per socket operation; enforce a total deadline yourself if you need one.

equivalents: Same idea in Go: `&http.Client{Timeout: 500 * time.Millisecond}` — covers connect, redirects and body read; zero means no timeout.
Same idea in Node.js: `fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(500) })` rejects with a TimeoutError.
Same idea in gRPC: set a deadline per call (none by default); expiry fails with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED and deadlines can propagate downstream.

title: Idempotency keys: exactly-once effect over at-least-once delivery
description: Show retries causing duplicate charges, then fix them with an Idempotency-Key header and a server-side dedupe store.
outcome: You can make a POST safe to retry: client sends a unique key per operation, server stores key+fingerprint+response and replays it.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only; no network access needed beyond localhost. macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (install: lesson 1)
overview: When a response is lost the client cannot tell whether the charge happened; it must retry, so the server must recognise the retry.

glossary.meaning: Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once (GET, PUT, DELETE are; POST, PATCH are not).
A unique client-generated value (e.g. UUID) identifying one logical operation across retries.

Keep resending until acknowledged; duplicates are possible.

concepts: Same logical operation → same key on every retry; new operation → new key.
Server: first time → process and store the response; retry after completion → replay stored response; retry while in progress → 409; same key, different payload → 422; missing key → 400.

code:
"""L100 (python idempotency.py): retries + lost responses = duplicate charges. Fix: Idempotency-Key
header + server-side dedupe store -> exactly-once *effect* over at-least-once delivery. Seeded."""
import hashlib, json, random, re, threading, urllib.request, uuid
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError

from helpers import OPENER, QuietHandler, serve  # plumbing: quiet handler, reply(), server thread

KEY_RE = re.compile(r'^"([0-9a-f-]{36})"$')  # our published key format: quoted UUID string


class PaymentB(QuietHandler):
    enforce = False          # True -> require Idempotency-Key and dedupe
    ledger, store, lock = [], {}, threading.Lock()  # store = dedupe store: key -> fp/state/response
    rng, loss_rate = random.Random(3), 0.4  # seeded: which responses get "lost" on the network

    def do_POST(self):
        raw = self.read_body()
        fingerprint, key = hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key")
        if self.enforce:
            if not (m := KEY_RE.match(key or "")):  # key missing/malformed -> 400
                return self.reply(400, {"title": "Idempotency-Key is missing or malformed"})
            key = m.group(1)
            with self.lock:
                seen = self.store.get(key)
                if seen and seen["fp"] != fingerprint:  # same key, different payload -> 422
                    return self.reply(422, {"title": "Idempotency-Key is already used"})
                if seen and seen["state"] == "in-progress":  # original still running -> 409
                    return self.reply(409, {"title": "A request is outstanding for this key"})
                if seen:  # retry of a completed request: replay the stored response, no new charge
                    return self.reply(*seen["response"])
                self.store[key] = {"fp": fingerprint, "state": "in-progress"}  # first time
        with self.lock:  # the side effect: money moves
            self.ledger.append(json.loads(raw)["amount"])
            response = (201, {"charge_id": f"ch_{len(self.ledger)}"})
            if self.enforce:  # same lock as the charge: no window where a crash could duplicate
                self.store[key].update(state="done", response=response)
            lose_it = self.rng.random() < self.loss_rate
        if lose_it:  # lost response: charge committed, client never hears back -> outcome unknown
            self.close_connection = True
            return
        self.reply(*response)


def pay(url, amount, key=None, max_attempts=5):
    """At-least-once client: resend the SAME request (and SAME key) until it gets an answer."""
    headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json"}
    if key:  # one key per logical operation, created by the caller BEFORE this retry loop
        headers["Idempotency-Key"] = f'"{key}"'  # sf-string per the IETF draft
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, json.dumps({"amount": amount}).encode(), headers)
        try:
            with OPENER.open(req, timeout=2) as r:
                return r.status, json.load(r), attempt
        except HTTPError as e:
            return e.code, json.load(e), attempt
        except (URLError, ConnectionError):  # no response -> unknown outcome -> retry
            continue
    return None, None, max_attempts


def run(enforce, seed=1):
    PaymentB.enforce, PaymentB.rng = enforce, random.Random(3)
    PaymentB.ledger.clear(); PaymentB.store.clear()
    srv = serve(PaymentB)
    url, keys = f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_port}/charges", random.Random(seed)
    print(f"--- Idempotency-Key {'ON' if enforce else 'OFF'}: 5 orders x 10 ---")
    for order in range(1, 6):
        # Production: uuid.uuid4(). Seeded here only so the output is reproducible.
        key = str(uuid.UUID(int=keys.getrandbits(128), version=4)) if enforce else None
        status, body, attempts = pay(url, 10, key)
        print(f"order {order}: {status} {body} after {attempts} attempt(s)")
    print(f"ledger: {len(PaymentB.ledger)} charges, total {sum(PaymentB.ledger)} (expected 50)")
    if enforce:
        print("reuse key with amount 99 ->", pay(url, 99, key)[:2])
        print("no key at all            ->", pay(url, 10)[:2])
    srv.shutdown(); srv.server_close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(enforce=False)
    run(enforce=True)

title: Ordering events with Lamport clocks
description: Three nodes exchange messages with Lamport timestamps; skewed wall clocks mis-order events, Lamport order keeps cause before effect.
outcome: You can implement the three Lamport clock rules, attach timestamps to messages, and build a causally consistent total order with a node-id tie-break.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only; no network access needed beyond localhost. macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (install: lesson 1)
overview: Each node's wall clock is a little wrong, so timestamps from different nodes can put an effect before its cause; a Lamport counter carried on messages cannot.

glossary.meaning: Difference between two nodes' wall clocks at the same instant.
a → b if a is earlier on the same node, or a is a send and b its receive, or via a chain of these.
An integer counter per node: tick on every event, send it with messages, on receive take max(local, received)+1.
Neither happened-before the other; Lamport order between them is arbitrary.

concepts: Rules: local event → clock += 1; send → clock += 1 and attach clock; receive → clock = max(clock, msg_ts) + 1.
If a → b then L(a) < L(b); the reverse is NOT guaranteed.
Sort by (Lamport, node id) for a total order consistent with causality.

steps.expected: Wall-clock order: 2 causality violations. (Lamport, node) order: 0.

code:
"""L100 (python lamport.py): three nodes exchange HTTP messages carrying Lamport timestamps. Wall
clocks are skewed on purpose: sorting by wall time breaks cause->effect, Lamport order doesn't."""
import json, threading, urllib.request

from helpers import OPENER, QuietHandler, serve, show, violations  # plumbing + log printing

TRUE_TIME = [0.0]                                # simulated "real" time, +10 ms per event
SKEW_S = {"A": 0.000, "B": -0.080, "C": +0.040}  # clock skew: B runs 80 ms slow, C 40 ms fast
EVENTS = []                                      # (lamport, node, wall, text, msg_id)


class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.clock, self.lock, node = name, 0, threading.Lock(), self

        class Handler(QuietHandler):
            def do_POST(self):
                node.on_receive(json.loads(self.read_body()))
                self.send_response(204); self.end_headers()

        self.srv = serve(Handler)

    def record(self, text, msg_id=None):
        TRUE_TIME[0] += 0.010
        wall = round(TRUE_TIME[0] + SKEW_S[self.name], 3)  # what this node's own wall clock says
        EVENTS.append((self.clock, self.name, wall, text, msg_id))

    def local(self, text):
        with self.lock:
            self.clock += 1  # rule 1, local event: tick
            self.record(text)

    def send(self, other, text, msg_id):
        with self.lock:
            self.clock += 1  # rule 2, send: tick, then attach the timestamp to the message
            ts = self.clock
            self.record(f"send '{text}' to {other.name}", msg_id)
        body = json.dumps({"from": self.name, "ts": ts, "text": text, "id": msg_id}).encode()
        OPENER.open(urllib.request.Request(f"http://127.0.0.1:{other.srv.server_port}/msg", body,
                                           {"Content-Type": "application/json"}), timeout=2).close()

    def on_receive(self, msg):
        with self.lock:
            self.clock = max(self.clock, msg["ts"]) + 1  # rule 3, receive: max(local, received) + 1
            self.record(f"recv '{msg['text']}' from {msg['from']}", msg["id"])


def scenario(node_cls=Node):
    a, b, c = node_cls("A"), node_cls("B"), node_cls("C")
    a.local("user clicks Buy")
    a.send(b, "create order", "m1")
    b.local("reserve stock")
    b.send(c, "charge card", "m2")
    c.send(a, "payment ok", "m3")
    c.local("write audit log")
    a.local("show receipt")
    for n in (a, b, c):
        n.srv.shutdown(); n.srv.server_close()
    return EVENTS


if __name__ == "__main__":
    events = scenario()
    show("sorted by wall clock", sorted(events, key=lambda e: e[2]))
    # total order: (Lamport, node id) - consistent with causality; node id breaks ties
    show("sorted by (Lamport, node)", sorted(events, key=lambda e: (e[0], e[1])))

equivalents: Same idea in any language: an integer counter + a mutex per node, sent in a message header (e.g. an HTTP header or message metadata field).
Vector clocks / version vectors: one counter per node; detect concurrency, not just order.
gRPC avoids skew for deadlines by propagating a remaining timeout instead of an absolute time.

inRealSystems: Automerge's operation IDs are Lamport timestamps (counter, actor ID), compared by counter then actor ID; Apache Cassandra, by contrast, stamps writes with the coordinator's wall-clock time in microseconds by default, so clock skew matters there.
useWhen: Use Lamport clocks when you need an order that never puts an effect before its cause, e.g. merging logs from several nodes; avoid them when you must detect concurrency (use vector clocks) or need real elapsed time (use a monotonic clock locally).
simulatorVsReal: Wall clocks and their skew are simulated (a shared simulated 'true time' + fixed per-node offsets) so the output is reproducible; messages are real HTTP calls on localhost.
caution: Lamport order is consistent with causality, not with real time: L(a) < L(b) does not mean a happened first or caused b.
